interest: This file provides valuable historical insight into both U.S. naval intelligence surveillance of the Japanese-American community immediately following Pearl Harbor and high-level diplomatic posturing in Tokyo during late 1940. The ONI report is particularly significant for historians of the Japanese-American internment, as it reveals the nuanced yet suspicious intelligence assessments that characterized traditional immigrant mutual-aid associations (Kenjin Kai) as potential vectors for Japanese government influence while detailing their specific street addresses across California, Oregon, Washington, and Hawaii. Concurrently, the private letter from Thomas L. Blakemore offers an evocative, behind-the-scenes perspective on the America-Japan Society's December 1940 luncheon, contrasting Foreign Minister Matsuoka's aggressive rhetoric with Ambassador Grew's skillful diplomatic counter-punching in the final year before the outbreak of the Pacific War.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.43, covering September 1940 to February 1942) documents Japanese societies and bilateral cultural and political organizations operating in Japan and the United States on the eve of and during the opening months of World War II. The centerpiece of the file is an extensive February 1942 Counter-Intelligence Section report from the Office of Naval Intelligence evaluating Japanese prefectural, regional, and overseas societies (such as Kenjin Kai and Kaigai Kyokai) in the United States, investigating their historical ties to Japanese emigration, suspected links to Tokyo's wartime propaganda and financial appeals, and providing an extensive geographical directory of West Coast branches. The file also contains diplomatic correspondence and cross-reference records regarding the America-Japan Society in Tokyo, including Ambassador Joseph C. Grew's reports on leadership elections and high-profile diplomatic luncheons featuring Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka, as well as an eyewitness letter by American legal scholar Thomas L. Blakemore describing the interplay between Matsuoka and Grew as the bilateral relationship deteriorated.

subfiles.about: Transmittal memorandum forwarding an Office of Naval Intelligence study on Japanese prefectural, regional, and overseas societies to designated naval, military, and civilian intelligence agencies.
subfiles.from: The Chief of Naval Operations (J. B. W. Waller)
subfiles.summary: This confidential memorandum from the Chief of Naval Operations, signed by direction by J. B. W. Waller, transmits Enclosure A, titled 'Study of Japanese Prefectural, Regional and Overseas Societies.' The memorandum states that the study was prepared by the Counter-Intelligence Section of the Office of Naval Intelligence from internal investigations and is transmitted for information. Copies are distributed across senior naval commands as well as the War Department, FBI, State Department, Coordinator of Information, Department of Justice, and Treasury Department.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Chief of Naval Operations transmitting study of Japanese Prefectural, Regional and Overseas Societies

subfiles.about: Intelligence report examining the history, organization, activities, propaganda ties, and local branch directory of Japanese prefectural, regional, and overseas societies in the United States.
subfiles.from: Counter-Intelligence Section, Office of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.summary: This comprehensive intelligence study by the Counter-Intelligence Section of the Office of Naval Intelligence investigates the background and functions of Japanese prefectural, regional, and overseas organizations (Kenjin Kai, Kaigai Kyokai, etc.) in the United States and its territories. Drawing from the 'History of Japanese Residents in America' published by the Japanese Association of America, the study traces how these bodies originated around 1900 as mutual-aid societies before developing close ties with Japanese colonization bodies and government propaganda programs, including donations to Tokyo's war chest and participation in the 1940 2600th Anniversary Celebration. While observing pre-war moves by some branches to demonstrate American loyalty and post-Pearl Harbor voluntary disbandments, the report concludes that their members warrant suspicion due to high proportions of aliens, exposure to Tokyo propaganda, and leadership ties to detained individuals. The report concludes with an extensive geographic roster detailing dozens of prefectural and regional associations with their street addresses in California, Oregon, Washington, Utah, and Hawaii.
subfiles.title: Study of Japanese Prefectural, Regional and Overseas Societies

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting the election of officers, including Count Aisuke Kabayama as president, of the America-Japan Society in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports to the Secretary of State that the America-Japan Society held an election meeting on the previous day in Tokyo. Count Aisuke Kabayama was elected president, while Ryozo Asano and E. W. Frazar were elected vice presidents. The plain telegram was transmitted from Tokyo via Shanghai.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Grew (Tokyo) on election of officers of the America-Japan Society

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a telegram regarding speeches and comments delivered at an America-Japan Society luncheon.
subfiles.summary: This State Department cross-reference file note indexes Telegram No. 1340, dated December 19, 1940, sent from Tokyo by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew. The telegram quotes comments delivered during a luncheon of the America-Japan Society. The original document is filed under decimal file 711.94/1881.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 1340 from Grew on America-Japan Society luncheon

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a telegram reporting statements by Diet members at an America-Japan Society meeting regarding Japanese government policy to conciliate the United States.
subfiles.summary: This State Department cross-reference file note indexes Telegram No. 102, sent from Japan by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew on January 22, 1941. It notes that at a large gathering of the America-Japan Society, three members of the Diet reported that Japanese government policy announced in the Diet that day aimed to conciliate the United States. The original paper is filed under decimal file 711.94/1925.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 102 from Grew on Japanese Diet members at America-Japan Society

subfiles.about: Personal letter describing an America-Japan Society luncheon in Tokyo featuring speeches by Foreign Minister Matsuoka and Ambassador Grew.
subfiles.summary: Thomas L. Blakemore writes from Tokyo to Mr. Rogers describing how America-Japan Society luncheons had become vital diplomatic sounding boards. He recounts the December 19, 1940 luncheon attended by Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka, incoming Ambassador Kichisaburo Nomura, and returning Ambassador Kensuke Horinouchi, with Ambassador Joseph C. Grew presiding as toastmaster. Blakemore analyzes Matsuoka's carefully crafted defense of Japan's national expansionist aims and praises Grew's polished, extemporaneous rebuttal firmly upholding American objections to Japan's 'New Order.' The letter closes with personal notes about Blakemore's holiday plans and an upcoming skiing trip to Akakura near Lake Nojiri.
subfiles.title: Letter from Thomas L. Blakemore to Mr. Rogers regarding America-Japan Society luncheon

subfiles.about: Internal State Department administrative charge slip tracking loans and routing of the file jacket for File 894.43 Japan-America Society.
subfiles.summary: This Department of State charge slip tracks the checkout and custody history of the file jackets for File No. 894.43 (Japan-America Society). Entries record the transfer of jackets to the Division of Far Eastern Affairs (FE), Turner, and other personnel between July 1934 and December 1944, accompanied by clerks' initials and return dates.
subfiles.title: Charge slip for File 894.43 Japan-America Society

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet referencing an Osaka consular despatch on the political activities of Teiichi Muto and the organization 'Saisei'.
subfiles.summary: This State Department cross-reference file note indexes an unnumbered despatch dated April 13, 1940, from Consul John M. Allison in Osaka. The referenced despatch discusses the organizational and political activities of Tei-ichi Muto and his society 'Sai-sei' ('Saisei'). The original report is filed under decimal file 894.00/906.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for despatch from Allison (Osaka) on Teiichi Muto and 'Saisei'

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a telegram regarding the drafting of regulations for a new cultural and goodwill organization under Japan's 'new structure'.
subfiles.summary: This State Department cross-reference file note indexes Telegram No. 7865, sent from Tokyo by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew on September 19, 1940. It reports on the impending formation of a new goodwill and cultural organization under Japan's 'new structure' (shintaisei), noting that Admiral Ogasawara and Yamamoto of the YMCA were chosen to draft its regulations. The original telegram is filed under decimal file 894.918/36.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 7865 from Grew on new cultural and goodwill organization
